source.title: A Theory of Conditional Collapse under Low-Rank Weight-Space Ablations: I. The Single-Block Theory and Synthetic Validation

record.tranche_reason: The paper compares patching with weight-space ablation and gives an explicit construction where they disagree without any repair mechanism. This refines the attribution interpretation of self-repair; it does not test downstream compensation itself.
record.gate_note: The paper cites the Hydra effect but does not measure later components changing their outputs to restore a prediction. Its own relevant results compare patching and ablation, and measure interaction between a head ablation and its own layer's MLP; those are not direct measurements of self-repair or restoration.
record.test_reason: The study never measures self-repair, meaning later components changing their outputs to restore a prediction after an ablation. Its results compare patching with weight-space ablation in an idealized additive model and in small synthetic-task transformers. It shows that redundancy alone can make ablation understate importance and make patching overshoot (κ>1), 'with no repair mechanism at all'. That offers a non-repair route to the attribution gap V7 describes. But the paper does not argue that self-repair is absent or misattributed in language models. It cites the Hydra effect, and Gong et al.'s backup components, as consistent with its account. No row measures downstream compensation, so the study discusses V7's mechanism rather than testing any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that a negative ablation result is not, on its own, evidence that a component is unimportant, and a positive patch is not evidence that it is necessary, because the two interventions measure different quantities that redundant codes separate. They add that the idealization's failure is an interaction term of known order: exactly zero for MLP-only ablations and bounded at second order otherwise.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses low-rank weight-space edits on small transformers trained on synthetic conditional tasks and compares them with activation patching. It does not reproduce the original self-repair measurement of downstream compensation in language models.
record.method_sensitivity: The interaction/fidelity relationship is reported across different configuration sets and task/architecture: ρ = −0.83 over 39 marker-task configurations, −0.85 over 25 held-out marker-task configurations, and −0.90 over 15 configurations in the second task. The apparent interaction-magnitude separation band fails on held-out configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: In an additive carrier model, patching moves the readout by a carrier's contrast and ablation by its level at the receiver. With redundant carriers, every single patch flips the decision while no single ablation does, producing overshoot (κ>1) and apparent dispensability without any repair mechanism. A trained synthetic network shows the same pattern at one site (κ=1.043, 57% still correct after ablation).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Redundancy alone, without downstream compensation, can make ablation understate and patching overstate a component's importance, mimicking self-repair signatures.

fits_no_version.finding: Measured head–MLP interaction magnitude tracks, monotonically, how well the independent-carrier idealization predicts the edited network (ρ=−0.83, −0.85 held-out, −0.90 on a second task). A clean threshold fails out of sample.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger same-block nonlinear interaction is associated with worse agreement between additive-ablation predictions and edited-network behaviour.

record.problems: The empirical evaluation is on small transformers trained on synthetic tasks, not language models on natural text. The paper explicitly says it does not conduct a general empirical study. The clean interaction-magnitude threshold fails on further configurations, and the second task uses a single trained instance. The results do not directly measure downstream compensation or self-repair.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional collapse rates, robustness-certificate measurements, polarity reversals, and protocol-gap checks. These concern its synthetic conditional-collapse and measurement claims rather than the versions about downstream self-repair, so they were not included as rows.

untested.parts: No ablation of an attention layer with measurement of later layers' compensation.
No measurement of late-MLP downregulation of the top token or of how it changes under ablation.
No single-head ablations on general text, model families or sizes; only synthetic tasks.
No measurement of the size of self-repair, its per-prompt variability, or overcorrection.
No identification of backup heads, copy suppression, LayerNorm rescaling or anti-erasure neurons.
No comparison of mean or resample ablation against zero ablation; ablation is low-rank weight projection only.
No measurement of self-repair as the cause of ablation-score error. The study shows only that redundancy without repair can produce a similar patch/ablation gap.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's guess of relation 'tests'/T5 with V7 labels is not adopted. The paper's 'challenges' label conflated offering an alternative mechanism with evidence against self-repair; the paper itself treats the Hydra effect and backup components as consistent with its account. All experiments use small synthetic-task transformers, not language models on natural text. The record's gate_note was already right that self-repair is not measured.

versions.untested_parts: No test of ablating a language-model attention layer and measuring later attention layers' compensation or restoration.
No test of late MLP downregulation of a maximum-likelihood token or how it changes under earlier-component ablation.
No test of single attention-head ablations on the full output distribution across general text, model families, or sizes.
No measurement of prompt-wise self-repair variability or overcorrection relative to the direct ablation effect.
No test identifying backup heads, copy-suppression heads, final LayerNorm rescaling, or anti-erasure neurons as self-repair mechanisms.
No comparison of self-repair under mean, resample, or other on-distribution ablations versus zero ablation.

The study tests patching-versus-ablation disagreement, but does not test downstream self-repair as the cause of attribution error or measure an ablation-based importance score against a component's direct effect.

rows.subject: abstract conditional model construction (Corollary 4)
rows.operation_detail: Patch one carrier from donor to receiver in the explicit construction.
rows.measure: Receiver selector change and whether the patch flips the receiver
rows.value: Each patch changes the selector by βiδi = 3/2 and flips the receiver.
rows.note: The construction demonstrates patching/ablation dissociation without a repair mechanism; it is not evidence of downstream compensation.
rows.check: This is a mathematical construction (Corollary 4), not an empirical result. It shows a patch/ablation dissociation from redundancy with no repair mechanism, so it does not measure self-repair or an attribution error caused by it.

source_check.locator_found: Section 6, Corollary 4 and its explicit construction, p. 10.

rows.subject: abstract conditional model construction (Corollary 4)
rows.operation_detail: Ablate one carrier at a time in the explicit construction.
rows.measure: Receiver selector change and whether the ablation flips the receiver
rows.value: Each single-carrier ablation changes the selector by −βiαi(xB) = 1/2 and does not flip the receiver.
rows.note: The patch/ablation discrepancy arises from the different quantities they change, not from a repair mechanism.
rows.check: This is the ablation half of the same theoretical construction as r1, not a measurement. Self-repair is absent by construction, so the row cannot bear on V7's claim that self-repair causes misattribution.

source_check.locator_found: Section 6, Corollary 4 and its explicit construction, p. 10.

rows.subject: further instance of the same synthetic task (not otherwise named)
rows.operation_detail: Patch the first-layer MLP output site found by the patch search.
rows.measure: Median recovery κ and argmax flip rate
rows.value: Median κ = 1.043; argmax flip rate = 0.85. The text also reports values 1.04–1.22 on the pairs used for the search.
rows.locator: Section 8, “Patching versus ablation on the same site”
rows.note: The study describes recovery above 1 as the overshoot signature. This measures patching, not downstream restoration.
rows.check: The row measures patch recovery (κ=1.043) on a trained synthetic-task network, not downstream compensation after ablation. The subject is a further marker-task instance (4-layer, width-64 per the appendix), not a language model.

source_check.locator_found: Section 8, Patching versus ablation on the same site, pp. 15–16.

rows.subject: further instance of the same synthetic task (not otherwise named)
rows.operation_detail: Ablate the weights feeding the same first-layer MLP output site.

conditions.value: same first-layer MLP output site as r3

rows.measure: Receiver-format accuracy after ablation; share of answers that are correct or literal
rows.value: Receiver format remains correct on 57% of inputs; correct plus literal accounts for 0.993 of the answers.
rows.locator: Section 8, “Patching versus ablation on the same site”
rows.note: The authors call the site patch-sufficient but far from ablation-necessary. This shows a patch/ablation discrepancy, not that later components compensate.
rows.check: 57% receiver accuracy after ablation may reflect redundancy or downstream recomputation; the study does not separate the two or measure compensation. The un-ablated baseline is not given for this instance. 'Partial' has no referent without a linked version.

relation.reason: The introduction and related work discuss Hydra compensation and attribution, but the study's own results concern distinct intervention quantities and additive-model fidelity.

tranche.reason: The study establishes patching–ablation dissociation and interaction–fidelity relationships without measuring self-repair. Its redundancy construction does not show any claim version absent or reversed.

source_check.notes: Patch-recovery overshoot is not downstream compensation after ablation. The reading-list statement's study-specific findings are accurate; catalog-wide uniqueness, challenge counts, and comparisons with other records cannot be verified from the permitted sources.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The explicit conditional-model construction and the same-site synthetic-task patch/ablation comparison
reader_labels.reason: Patching and ablation give different indications of component sufficiency/necessity: r1–r4 show patch flips or overshoots while single-carrier ablation need not flip and the tested receiver remains correct on 57% of inputs.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: The paper shows that patch/ablation attribution disagreement can arise from redundancy and the different quantities the interventions change, without any repair mechanism; it therefore does not establish self-repair as the cause of such disagreement.
